questions.q: Define the term "degree of a relation" and state its value for the GUARDIAN relation shown in the NCERT textbook (Figure 7.5).
questions.a: Degree is the number of attributes (columns) in a relation. For GUARDIAN(GUID, GName, GPhone, GAddress) the degree is 4. A wrong answer (e.g., saying degree = 5 because there are 5 rows) reveals the student confuses degree (column count) with cardinality (row count) – a fundamental terminology swap that will cascade into errors when defining schemas or writing DDL.

questions.q: In the STUDENT relation, the attribute SDateofBirth has domain "set of all valid calendar dates". A student proposes storing "15th May 2003" as a VARCHAR string "15-May-2003". Explain why this violates the domain concept even though the value "looks like a date".
questions.a: A domain is a *set of values of a specific data type* (e.g., DATE), not just a semantic description. Storing dates as VARCHAR breaks the domain because: (1) the DBMS cannot enforce date validity (e.g., "31-Feb-2003" would be accepted), (2) date arithmetic (age calculation, sorting chronologically) fails, (3) the atomicity property is violated – the string "15-May-2003" has meaningful sub-parts (day, month, year) whereas a DATE value is atomic. A wrong answer shows the student thinks domain = "what the data means" rather than "the declared data type and its value set".

questions.q: The ATTENDANCE relation has attributes (AttendanceDate, RollNumber, AttendanceStatus). On 2018-09-01, RollNumber 3 (Taleem Shah) is marked 'A'. On 2018-09-02, the same RollNumber 3 is again marked 'A'. Are these two tuples distinct? Justify using Property 2 of relations.
questions.a: Yes, they are distinct tuples. Property 2 states "each tuple in a relation is distinct" – uniqueness is judged across *all* attributes of the tuple. The two tuples differ in AttendanceDate (2018-09-01 vs 2018-09-02), so the full tuple values differ. A student who says "they are duplicates because RollNumber and Status are same" misunderstands that tuple identity requires *all* attribute values to match, not just some – this confusion leads directly to primary key design errors in the next node.

questions.q: Compare the STUDENT file in Table 7.1 (file system) with the STUDENT relation in Table 7.4 (relational model). Identify two structural differences that illustrate Property 1 and Property 3 of the relational model.
questions.a: Property 1 (attribute uniqueness & sequence immaterial): In Table 7.1 the file has columns "RollNumber, SName, SDateofBirth, GName, GPhone, GAddress" – but GName/GPhone/GAddress are guardian attributes mixed with student attributes, violating "each attribute has a unique name" in the context of a single relation. In Table 7.4, STUDENT has only student attributes plus GUID (foreign key), each with a unique name. Property 3 (atomic values, same domain per column): Table 7.1 stores guardian phone as "5711492685" (10-digit) but also "S -13, Ashok Village, Daman" in GAddress – mixed formats in one column if extended. Table 7.4 enforces atomic, single-domain values per attribute. A wrong answer indicates the student sees only "columns vs rows" not the formal constraints that make a *relation* different from a *file*.

questions.q: A school database designer argues: "Since NULL means 'value unknown', we should allow NULL in the RollNumber attribute of STUDENT because a new student might not have been assigned a roll number yet." Evaluate this argument using the relational model rules.
questions.a: The argument is invalid. RollNumber is the primary key (implied by uniqueness requirement). Property 2 requires every tuple to be distinct; a primary key attribute *cannot* be NULL because NULL ≠ NULL in SQL (unknown ≠ unknown), so two tuples with NULL RollNumber would violate tuple uniqueness. Moreover, the NCERT text explicitly states: "Since each student shall have one unique roll number, we can put the NOT NULL and UNIQUE constraints on the RollNumber column." A wrong evaluation shows the student treats NULL as just "another value" rather than a special marker that breaks equality comparisons and key constraints.

questions.q: Design a minimal relation schema for a "LIBRARY_BOOK" entity that captures: book identification, title, author, publication year, and current status (available/issued). Specify relation name, attribute names, plausible domains, degree, and cardinality for a library with 12,000 books. Explain why your design satisfies Property 3 (atomicity and domain consistency).
questions.a: Relation: LIBRARY_BOOK(BookID, Title, Author, PubYear, Status). Domains: BookID → INTEGER (or VARCHAR for ISBN), Title → VARCHAR(100), Author → VARCHAR(50), PubYear → INTEGER (1000..2025), Status → ENUM('available','issued') or CHAR(1) with CHECK constraint. Degree = 5. Cardinality = 12,000. Property 3 satisfied because: each attribute draws from a single domain (no mixed types), each value is atomic (Title is not split into subtitle/series here; Author is single string – though in practice we might normalize further, at this level it's atomic), no attribute holds multiple values per tuple (Status is single-valued), NULL allowed only where meaningful (e.g., PubYear might be NULL for ancient books). A poor answer lists attributes without domains, confuses degree/cardinality, or allows multi-valued Status like "available, issued, reserved" in one field.
